blocks.x: The best thing to do is to get everybody's name down. Could you give us your full name? Benjamin. Is it F or anything? Franklin. Franklin. Lord, what's your name?
Lord, it's a good name.
My name is Dick Allen. And what's today's date, Jim? February?
Ninth.
Yeah, it's the ninth.
Ninth, yeah.
Yeah, nineteen...
Seventy-two.
And where are we? What's the address here?
218 Slidell Street, Algiers. And Algiers.
And this is your home here.
You own your own house? Oh, my own home.

Got a nice crystal chandelier up there. Thank you. It's a beautiful home. Thank you very much. It's nicely decorated and painted and everything. So, uh... Can you tell us a little bit about your life, where you were born and all that sort of thing?
I was born in Algiers. Nineteen and seven. Nineteen and seven. Maybe thirteen, nineteen and seven. Mm-hmm.
And, uh, what about your family? Were there any musicians in there?

Well, my mother played in those pianos, the churches, you know. My grandmother, and I had an aunt, but she played in the church. But there wasn't a professional, you know. She played music. But, yeah, I'm going to say that.
What church did you do?
Well, uh, she never played in the church. Nobody plays church music.
Oh, I see. Did she play at home? Uh-huh. At home, you know. I had an aunt, she used to play at home. She didn't listen to music instead.
And...
And your uncle, what did he play?
Yeah. We all played with it, yeah.
Mm-hmm. So that runs in your, uh, pattern?
Yeah, yeah, we... I didn't hear what that is.
Yeah. And how did you get into it?

Well, uh... Well, I... I was about nineteen... What happened? Well, I was born. Mm-hmm. And my daddy bought a piano, you see. And, uh, I was always interested in music. So I started to practice around the house on the piano. And finally, I began to be more interested in it. So I flew around and started playing little house chords. And then I improved on it. And then I started playing little house chords. I took the book, book cards. There were a lot of these drummers out that time. And then I was called the work of the track one. And then Freddie Coleman. It was called by the name of, uh... Stanley Williams. He was in Chicago now. I don't know if he was still playing. Another guy. Bill Conley. What did they play? All drummers, I wanted to call them. Wilford Bullcott's saxophone, and Teddy Johnson, you might know him. He did saxophone. He did saxophone. Yeah, yeah. Well, he used to get three or four pieces like that to go to house parties. And from there, I started getting a little larger jobs, so I had to increase the band. Well, we didn't have an organized band. I played at Midway in Harvey one night, and so I needed about seven pieces. I don't remember all the guys that played at the time, but I know Wilford was one of them. I think Wilford played drum, and we were playing drum at the time, but Wilford played saxophone, and a fellow by the name of Remy Trumpet, and I hired a guy by the name of George Augustine to play a banjo. He was playing banjo at the time. And he was a member of a band that called Slumber South Syncope. And that was mostly beginning of me playing professionally. But before that, I played around with Kit Tormus and all the jobs on this side. I had never played on the other side, but I was. And I started taking this and I'm the manetta. And he said, the first job that he set me on on the other side of the river was at the halfway house. It's been quite a while now. I just remember who all the musicians were that I played with at that time. But at the beginning of playing on that side, it was my first job.
Where is the halfway house?
That was back at Canal Street there. Somewhere not far from the New Orleans Country Club. Oh, I know the place.
That's the one I was thinking about. It's an Orkin place. Yeah, that's what it is now?

Yeah. Yeah, but that's the first job, professional job I've been. How old were you then? Oh, I must have been around about... I'm in my twenties, I know. About twenty, twenty-two, twenty-three, something like that.
Who was this Remy guy?

He was just playing trumpet. Well him and myself, Wilford Boccage, and let's see, I was on piano, he was on trumpet, Wilford Boccage, saxophone, and I think Ernest Lewis would play at the Kitto at the time.
I never heard of him.
No, he didn't play for him. He was different. He used to just play a rock and all this stuff.
When you say that you started playing professionally, you mean that you didn't have any other job? You had no day job?
No, I started playing professional musicians.
Oh, but you still had another job?
No.
I mean supporting yourself, yeah.

No, well I was out in school. Oh, you were still in school? Yeah, I was still in school then, you see. Well, I was going at my town in thirty-five when I was beginning of it, you understand? I was going to have a sort of playing, I was in school.
And when you left school, did you go into some other kind of work or did you just-
No, I played music then. Just music, that's all. Just music then, you see.
How long did you keep doing that before you started having that job?
Well, I started playing job in 1939.
So up till then you just played music? Yeah, before that.

Up until 1939 I just played music for a living. I see. Well, you know, like I played with the Sonny South Syncopated, I was an organized band. Most of my job was mostly with ten piece artists, you know, large bands. And I worked with them for quite a while. I started with the Sonny South Syncopated in 1928.
That's a reading band, huh?

Reading band, yeah. We had ten pieces, eleven pieces with the piano. Who was he meant to? We had Lee, a fellow by the name of Lee, playing voice alto, I mean third alto, Emile Fritz tenor, Elliot Taylor, voice sax, Richard McNein, guitar, a fellow by the name of Charles, bass, Sently J, trumpet. Who? Sently J, Anthony Sently J.
Yeah, I never did know him.
No, you didn't know him. You got out the picture.
Leo Dejom, I don't know if you know him.

Who I heard of the trumpet player. The trumpet player, Leo Dejom. That's Harold's brother. Yeah, and the drummer was a fellow by the name of Gilly. I don't know if you know him. That's the original Sonny South band. Gilly, songs about Dejom and myself on piano. You sang, huh? You were a singer, huh? No, Dejom was a song. Oh, you didn't sing at all.
I didn't sing at all.
Just played. I played.
I played. I played.
I played. I played. I played.
I played. I played. I played. Well, Leo was a singer? No, Leo Dejom, yeah.
He was a singer. Yeah, I see.
Did that band play mostly over here and there? All over. Well, he played on the other side, too, huh? Yeah, we played on the other side.

Well, we were just organized at that time, you see. Well, to get back to George August there, that's how did he get to his band. So I hired him out playing at the Midway in Harvard, you see. And I hired him to play with us. And he liked the way I played. And he said, man, you're the kind of man I need. I had a fellow playing at this band, under the name of Aston Murray. But he was mostly of lead, you know. He plays lead and didn't give him no support. And so he was a man like supporting the band, you know. And he found out how to read orchestrations and things like that. And he said, you're the man that you need somebody to give the band support. At that time, you know, a lot of guys, leads all through the music, they didn't want that. They had enough instruments for solo work and things like that. So mostly he wanted a man to work for the rhythm. Yeah, a rhythm man. So he liked my playing. So he told me that I said, give me your address and say, I'm not promising anything right now, I said, but in the near future, if anything happens to the other fellow, I'll be glad to have you. About six or seven months after that, he called me up. He told me to come to rehearsal and I went and started rehearsing with him. But we didn't have too much weight then because we just had organized, you see. So I started rehearsing with him, then Pierron started getting us a little job. And Pierron started getting us a little job working as him. And finally, we started broadcasting at WWWL, Coast to Coast, and that just brought us up.
Hmm, that's something, Coast to Coast. Yeah, Coast to Coast, yeah. I don't know, I lost those records.

I wanted to always keep them, you know, before the clips, you see. Oh, you had records? I had records of it from the station, Captain Pritchett was at the head of WWL at that time. Anybody know him, Captain Pritchett? No, I haven't. He was on Tulane, I mean, yeah, Tulane. You remember the school up there?
That's where I work at Tulane.
Yeah, you remember what I mean, my school. And Loyola. Yeah, used to broadcast from Loyola at that time.
I don't have to tell you. Well, you had the records from that? That's the thing.
Well, I had some telegrams and things from different parts, you know, different parts of the states, different states, you know. Oh, yeah.
But did you record? No, not at that time.
No, you didn't make any discs?
I didn't make no discs, no.
I made discs with Celestair when he was traveling. I played in Jeanette's play, you know Jeanette.
Yeah.
Kimber.
Where did you make the records?

Well, Mobile, there's no town, you know, if you had a town like that, you know. No, I made the first record with Peter on it. Not Peter on it, Peter Bocard. That's the only one I remember. But we broadcast from the states.
Oh, I see. Just stop for a while and see if it's recording okay.

Yeah, because I think it's picking up. Okay. Yeah, what were we talking about? Talking about you recording with Bocard. Yeah, Bocard, Bocard, Bocard, yeah. That's the mix. The only ones I remember recording. Just at one time? Yeah. Mama's going goodbye and, uh, go to the river to the car. Mm-hmm. Yeah, you were there.
Yeah, I was there for that. Yeah. What happened after you played with the Sunday South fans? Well, uh, how long did you play with them after that?
Yeah, in the middle thirties I live.

Anywhere, right, a little before Prohibition Indies. I was working with the and I was working with the and uh, how I could work with Celestate a while because Jennet Kimball, she was about a different family here. And so we made a swap. Mm-hmm. So she played in the Sunday South but now I must not play with Celestate. And now I must be traveling with the wrong way to the south. He didn't want to travel to? No, I want to travel to the wrong way to the south. But he didn't want to travel to? No, I want to travel to the condition, you see. So she worked in town with our band because we mostly worked in town. Mm-hmm. And Celestate was booked all, you know, all over Louisiana, Texas, Florida, Mississippi, Alabama. And they went all through Arkansas but I took six to them that time and I couldn't make a trip to Arkansas. So I had to stay home and want a peace show with them. Yeah. And around 30, right after Prohibition ended. Well that began the end of the large day. Mm-hmm. And so I had to stay home and want a peace show with them. And all these little, uh, uh, uh, uh, paragraphs and things started to end up, you see. Well, before that, uh, uh, Can I ask you a question? Yeah.

Can I ask you something about that, that, uh, I hate to interrupt you about this and we can come back to that time, uh, the end of Prohibition, but what did the band leader want? You said they didn't want to lead, they wanted support, huh? Did they want, did they want you to play softly or loud or what?

No, mostly a compromise, a orchestration music. Mm-hmm. See, I got a lot of it back there now from the band that we played, you see. I kept it just for a little span of it. Mm-hmm. A lot of those old numbers, you know, that we used to play. You'd read it, huh?
You'd play the, yeah.
Oh, I was. Did they want you to play heavy or light? Well, they'd perform heavy, but I never got a real rough piano player, you know. I must have played on the light side.
Well, I looked, I know Ashton Murray, I believe, is the same man. He's a little brown-skinned fellow.
Yeah.

From downtown. From downtown. I think he and Danny Barber got started together. I think Danny introduced him to him. Yeah. But he seems a little, you know, like he'd be delicate, you know, he's not a strong man.

No, well he mostly stuck to the music, you see. He couldn't memorize or nothing like that. You see, and everything that he wanted to play, he had to have the music for it, you see. He couldn't memorize it.
The Sonny South band, he played mostly Stocker and Jackson. Father Spearsman, yeah, Stocker and Jackson. He didn't have any range in the band.
No, you might know this guy, Caesar. At that time, he was very good with the range. Saxon. Saxon, yeah. And Sonny Johnson, yeah, Sonny Johnson. He was with the band, too. I never had met Sonny.
Never met John, boy.
He was with the saxophone. He was with the band, too. He played with the Sonny South a while. So he arranged. Huh? Yeah, he was a ranger and Caesar was a ranger. And we bought from different guys.
Was Caesar-
I don't think we bought him a side chord or a ranger. Side chord, you know him, don't you?
Yeah. Well Caesar was on saxophone and arranging both, huh? Well he wasn't playing with us.

He was a saxophone player, but he wasn't playing with us. He used to arrange for us, you see. We'd ring them bells and there were several good numbers we bought. He used to play with the trombone. Who was playing trombone? Eddie Pearson. I know you know him. Oh yeah. But he was another guy who helped me to get into Sonny South. He was playing, I forgot to tell you about the trombone, but he was playing trombone in the Sonny South.
But he's an Algerian.
Yeah, he's an Algerian. Yeah, he's an Algerian.
Yeah, well you all stuck together somehow, the Algerians, that would help each other out?
No, not Eddie, not Eddie, but with the bull cars. You know him. Never met him.
Is he alive?
That's the guy, I don't think he was on that recording. He's dead now. He's dead several years.
Peter I knew, and Charlie I knew, but I never knew Henry.

Charlie. Well Henry was in California. He left the band and went to California. And that's how we had John Porter playing, well that's a different band at the time, that was Creole Serenade. And then to get back to the Sonny South, well, a little before, I think it was Apple tradition or I'm not sure, but anyway, they had a little misunderstanding of Peter I was band. So they're fired, Peter Bull Kies, Charlie, and I don't know if he was born in the middle of the middle, but I think it was three or four of them. And then taking Leo Dejong from us, Eddie Pearson, and I think I was a tailor, formed another band. We'd use the same middle but it was three additions. So that made us have to get George McCollum started playing trumpet with us, Mike Neal playing trumpet.
One of them was playing trombone after the other there.
But they had the original band with the exception of Lewis.
So they went to Peel's band? Yeah, they went to Peel's band.

So what happened with Peter Bocas and them? Peter Bocas? He started his own band then. And we had the original Sonny South, you see. And then we had to get, I think, St. Johnson started playing with us then. And Sidney Montague was on the drum. And then we had another city too. Sidney Fluency, guitar. That was there in the Deceyne, in the Sonny South band. We worked a while with that band. And then that's where I started to play these clubs and band the Spanish. Then I started to stay in those spot jobs around the city. And I got a bit of rain here. I think I got a bit of rain here and stuff playing as a jujitsu tutor.
Oh, by the way, before you get there, who was the leader of the Sonny South band? Bill Dejauw. Bill Dejauw.
What did George Augustine have to do with it?
George Augustine?
Yeah.

Well at the time, see I don't know whether he was managing the band at the time, that he talked to me or not, but he had something to do with it I know. But he was the original Sonny South. He died too.
I see, but they had another guitar player in there when you were with the Sonny South. Yeah, Richard McLean. No, I played with George and Wilde, you see.
I see.
I got confused on that one.

Yeah, I played with George Augustine and Wilde with the band, and the voice band. Richard came after George. After George left the band. Then you went to what band? I left South the band was a small combination, you know. Oh, that's right. Kid Ranee, and the Chipsy T room. Kid Ranee's brother, I'm Joe Ranee. I was on the piano. I played Roy, Roy Evans on the drums, about four pieces. You didn't have any parents, no Reed or? Oh yeah, uh, oh, yes. Okay, of course, that's what I played. Now you had- Delarose. Oh. Delarose, you might know him. I know Walter. Walter Delarose.
That's the same guy?
That's the same guy.
We all- I know there's several guys in that family that play with him.
Yeah, Delarose.
What's that, was that still in the 30s you talking about?
Well, no, let's see.
It's up in the 40s.
That's pretty much, you know, we'll get a good- Well, when were- Where were you playing when the World War II broke out? 43? No, 43.
I was playing with Peter Brookhatt just a few or so.
But this is before then? Before then? Mm-hmm. I mean, this Rene Band, that was before you started with Brookhatt.
Oh yeah, that was before I started. Yeah, that probably was before the war.
Yeah. Maybe in the late 30s or something.
That's from between the 30s or close to the 40s.
Did you have different drums with Rene, or did you always use Joe Rene?
Joe Rene always played with his brother.
Yeah, I see. How long did you play with him? Oh, about two years or three years or something. Just in one place where you-
One at Gypsy Tea Room, yeah. And I worked, got a little spot job. And I worked-
Was that every night?

Every night. At Gypsy Tea Room? At Gypsy Tea Room, we used to work every night. We wait there until he began to improve his business, began to improve, you see. And so he began to substitute large bands. You know, he started getting so large, the business was doing so well in the business, so he started bringing in large bands. And so, by doing that for us, it looked like they didn't like it so much, and we shut them out of the job. So they were all just there in that band.
I wanted to ask you, did you ever work with Earl Barnes?
Not Earl Barnes, Paul Barnes. Oh, Paul Barnes. Yeah, I worked with Paul Barnes. He worked with Jitney Dance. Mm-hmm.
Is that before the Gypsy Tea Room or after?

That was after the Gypsy Tea Room. I went there afterwards. I went to, I think the original was Jim Robinson, Howard, Ken Howard, Paul Barnes. The drummer was Davis, the drummer, Eugene, or I knew he was playing.
Oh, he was a piano player. Davis was his last name?
Yeah, Davis was his last name.
He was Jimmy Davis' brother?
Jimmy Davis, yeah, he was playing after Lalu and all that stuff. Jimmy Davis' brother?
Jimmy Davis' brother.

I think he died. He was playing after Lavella, a classy dance hall. And a guitar? Guitar, he got killed. You know Walter Decker or Becker? Yeah. But he was one of the Walter killed him. Oh, Butler, right. Gae. Gae, yeah. He was playing banjos at the time. Anyway, but after you left Kidney you went to Piron's band, I mean to Pitebuka's band.
After you left Kidney, you went to Piron's band? I mean to Pitebuka's band.
Yeah. After you left Kidney, you went to Piron's band.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Wasn't that in your song?

Yeah, but I was working at the Lavella before. Oh, that was in between. Yeah, that was in between. I see. See, Pitebuka's band was the last band I was with. Oh, I see. I worked at the Lavella. Before I went to the Lavella I started working with Willie O'Connor.
You know Willie O'Connor. I never have Manning. Where does he play?
He was a guitar player. He worked at the entertainers, a colored player. He played some French songs.
He played some French songs.

He played some French songs. He played some French songs. In that band they had a guy named Cyril with saxophone, and Roy Evans, who's a drum, Willie O'Connor, guitar. I was playing piano, and Anderson, Big Anderson, playing trumpet. And Sam Lee was a tennis player. He was a tennis player. He was a big Anderson. Andy, yeah. Andy, yeah, Big Anderson. He's not big anymore. No. He's smaller.

He's getting smaller. He used to be fat, huh? Yeah. I think after he had his car accident in the last couple of weeks. I didn't know that, you see. Yeah, he's not big anymore. He's a big guy, and I was working with him. It's funny they call him big, and I can't even think who you mean because he's small now.
Juggy. Yeah? Jughead. You call him Jughead? No, we always call him Anderson, you know.
Andy.
Andrew Anderson was a real man. Yeah, yeah. Well, now he's Jughead. He was at the La Vida band. Who was running that band? Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor.
Now that's at the entertainment.
What does entertainment mean? Yeah, entertainment, yeah. Willie O'Connor and the Riffles. You see?
I thought Kid Kaifer was in there for a while.
I think Kaifer played there for a while, too. But I wasn't there. You weren't there, huh? No, I wasn't there when Kaifer played. Did you know Kaifer?
Yeah.
Kaifer and I played. That's another guy we used to play with, too, over here. He's from this side?
He's from this side.

He's in Gretman. Yeah, he's a pretty good trumpet player. He left me with Detroit. Well, he used to get a group together, like when you get a job. We didn't have a real organized band. We got a job with our high, Kaifer, Freddie Coleman, Wilbur Burkard, and maybe get somebody else from the other side, you know.
Was he any kind to Willie Kaifer? Did you ever know Willie Kaifer? I don't know Willie Kaifer. He was a musician? Yeah. He was a trumpet player and Henry Rush was telling me about him.
Yeah, well that's another guy. Yeah. And I worked with Henry Rush with Kit Thomas. Oh yeah? Yeah.
When were you working with Thomas? That was way early in your career? Yeah, it was kind of early in my career. You never worked in his band in later years?

No. You see, well, Kit Thomas and the guy they called Elton, well I didn't know this until afterwards. It was Kit Thomas' band, but Elton was running the band. You see, we all started with Elton's band until they had some kind of misunderstanding, and they split. So he had to change the name from Kit Thomas to another name, you see. So that's when I started playing with them. They always called him Kit Thomas.

Morgan told me he was in the band and they had real trouble, Andrew Morgan, said he had a lot of trouble with the telephone then. Because the phone was in Elton Paredo's house, is that right? Yeah, that's what I'm talking about.

See, in other words, Kit Thomas was the real owner of the band. But Elton used to run the band, you see, so all the business was transacted through Elton. Yeah. Well that's the same way it was with the Sonny South. You see, I wasn't managing nothing, but I wasn't working, I wasn't doing nothing, playing music, and other guys was working, and so I used to transact all the business, you know, get jobs like that, transfer to Leo or McNeil. I would contact them and have them go check the guy who's never called, you see. Who is McNeil now?
What's his name?
Uh, McNeil, he's a trumpet player, he was named at the Sonny South Symphony.
Well we can ask somebody. We'll ask him. You don't know his first name. Well, I forget his first name.
Alvin, Alvin, Alvin, Alvin, Alvin was McNeil.

Well anyway, back to what we were talking about the telephone. What Morgan told me was that the phone was under the name of Kid Thomas, and was in Elton Theodore's house. That's right. So now Thomas has the phone under the name of Thomas Valentine. Yeah, and it caused a real mix-up.
Yeah, you see, it was going in Kid Thomas at that time, and then when they changed it, they put it in Valentine's.
Yeah. Well nobody can phone up Kid Thomas now unless they know his right name. That's right.
Nobody knew him about Valentine. No. I didn't know that either, as long as I didn't know any more of my days. I didn't know his children saw Valentine until then.
Well how would you look up Kid Twat in the phone book?
Well, I don't know his telephone number. I know where he used to live. Would he be under T or Kid?
Oh, Joseph Butler.
Oh, Joseph Butler.
Oh, I see.

This brother has so many nicknames, yeah, Kid Twat. Joseph Butler. Did you have a nickname too? Outside of Benny. Everybody calls him Benny Tony. Everybody got nicknames. You know, I never have understood how people look each other up in the phone book if they
don't know their names.

Well when I joined, I was playing the Genetsch Players with Celestate, well they had nicknames. I came in the band, they all had some kind of nicknames so they didn't know what they called me, you see. So it wasn't God, I just remember what God was. See I used to name him Whipple. You remember Whipple, him, and the funny thing, and the Popeye, well that's what they named me Whipple. And every time they used to call me Whipple or Freddie used to call me Egg all the time. Freddie Coleman. Yeah, he was in the band. No he wasn't with us, but he was just giving me a nickname. He called you Egg. Yeah, Egg. The other guy used to call me Whipple. Why did they call you Egg? Oh I don't know, Whipple, Egg, you know.
Well the Celestan band had a lot of guys in it then or was it a small band?
No, Celestan was all, I can tell you at that time there were three big bands, Celestan, Sidney Desbenes, Sonny South, Pierron, all the guys from 10 to 11 there. Yeah, yeah.
Did you ever play with, we talked to all of the losers in the last week or so, Peter Lacazze, did you ever play with him?
No, I don't remember playing with him. But all the regular guys, Nelson, the trombone player, George Nelson. That's his brother, huh?
What?

George Nelson. George Nelson, that's a trombone player. Oh. Lewis Nelson, I think you know about Lewis. Yeah, Lewis Nelson. Lewis Nelson, yeah. Well I worked with him when he was in Sidney's band. You were with Sidney too? You played with Sidney too? Yeah, Substitute's like, you know. Yeah, I worked with him. Talking about Nelson, didn't you play with Big Al Lou Nelson too? Yeah, Big Al Lou I played with Sidney too. When did that happen? That was later on, huh? Well that was around in the forties. Yeah.
Yeah, in the forties.
I think that was after I came up to the service, I believe in the forties, something like that.
Yeah, it would have been after the service, but it's only a picture in a book.
Yeah. Go back to when, before you went into the service, you know, and I played with Sidney's band.
Who were you working with then, after the La La Vida band?
Well I was working with the Creole Serenators then. Uh huh. I see. I was working with the Creole Serenators.
Who was in that band then?

The Creole Serenators? They had, the piano player was Newman. Oh yeah. Yeah, you remember Newman. But he died. I never knew him. He played with him in the Adolf, a big Brownstein fella, his name was Adolf something, I forget his other name. He played with him a while.
What did he play?

Piano. Adolf and the guy just called, he was a piano player. Dwight Newman? Dwight Newman, yeah, he died. And Adolf died too. But he had Louie Warner playing sax, and Pete was playing trumpet, and his brothers playing guitar, and Williams. Yeah, drumming.
Like Alfred?
Alfred Williams, yeah. Alfred Williams. That was a little smaller band.
The smaller band, he had six pieces, five or six pieces.
Adolf, huh?
That guy's name was Adolf, huh?
The piano player? Yeah, I forget, I don't know, I forgot his last name.
Well what did Adolf Ducanje play? Was he a trumpet player, or what did you? Well, Ducanje. I know there were a lot of Ducanje.
I'm trying to think now, I don't know his name was Ducanje or not.
Peep played clarinet and sax. Peep Ducanje.
Peep Ducanje.
But I can't keep that family straight.
Yeah, you see it's been so long it kind of confused you.
Yeah, I forget all those names.
Is Peter Bocas playing on his trumpet then? He played violin too.

He played violin too. See now when Steve quit Piron's band, I used to supplicate in that band too. Oh he quit the band, Steve. Yeah he quit the band, he opened up a place sometime called a peak pen. You might have heard of him. Yeah. Where was that? He got it down there. No, he opened it up himself.
Oh, he wasn't playing then. Who? Steve. Did he play that or? Yeah he played that.

Oh I see him. Did he have a band? Yeah. That's where we left off. Yeah, I think that's where we left off. Who was in the band besides Steve? All the ones I remember was Steve Lewis and Jonathan Sears. We left Piron's band, the peak pen, that's the only one I remember.
Okay.
I can't remember what we were talking about.

Yeah, well I was quick on that. I would always follow them. I didn't care what they played. I knew it was progressive pretty well. I was having trouble. That's another thing that they liked. Anything they played, most likely I could play whether I knew it or not, it was progressive, unless it was a difficult number like Body and Soul or something like that. But you did learn some songs from music. Oh, getting to your eyes, numbers like that, I might have to hear the music, but just a little round number, whatever, I didn't worry about nothing like that. Mario Minera was the one who taught you to music? Yeah, he taught me. And he was the one who gave me the first job. The first job I would play with professionals. There was more of a four pieces to that, to a halfway house back at the Mel Street. I taught them.
I know they gave you this job.
Yeah, he gave me. He set me on that job. I don't remember who the musicians was at the time, but he set me on that job.
Did you ever play any other instruments that came?

Well, I tried the guitar, but I never could make it. I played a few chords on it. I loved guitar, and I wanted to take lessons, but I never did get around to it. But that was my next instrument, if I was, you know, I just loved that instrument, but I never did get around to it.
What kind of guitar did you like? Did you like chords, the lead, or picking?

Well, I didn't play with it long enough to remember myself with what style I would like. But I just liked it, period, to get there. But I think I would prefer the chord style, something like a Charlie Christian style. I see Pixie a lot too, but I read it in the chord style.
You mentioned some band was Sales, and I've forgotten which one.

That was Sidney, Sidney Desmond. He got a 11 piece band too. Did you play with them too? You know, substitute, because you piano play. I never was a regular man in this band. But my regular band that I really played in was Sonny South Syncopators, and Creole Serenators, Willow County Rippers, and Hannes, but I called it Hannes Seekers. I worked with Louis Duhmann on several bands.
When did you work with Louis Duhmann? Oh, yeah, quite a while. That's in the 40s still, or?
Before that. Before that.
When was that now? Oh man, that's quite a while. Way back. Yes, way back, yeah.
Before you played with the Sonny South?

Yeah, I think it was before I played with the Sonny South, way back. Who was in his band? Would you remember any of that? One of my cousins was trombone. Oh yeah? I used to call him Yankee. That's your cousin? Yeah, you know him. You know him? No, I heard all about him. Johnson, his name was. He's related to you? Yeah, that's my cousin. Oh yeah?
That's my wife's, RT's husband.

segments.chapter: Opening and background
segments.title: Recording setup: names, date and location in Algiers
segments.summary: Dick Allen gets the names and date (9 Feb 1972) and the address of Turner's home in Algiers.

segments.chapter: Opening and background
segments.title: Born in Algiers, 1907; mother and relatives played music at home
segments.summary: Turner says he was born in Algiers in 1907. His mother, grandmother and aunt played piano at home but not professionally.

segments.chapter: Early years and the Sonny South
segments.title: Father's piano, house-party bands and first job at the Halfway House
segments.summary: His father bought a piano and he taught himself. He formed small house-party groups with Wilford Boccage and others, and his first professional job across the river was at the Halfway House.

segments.chapter: Early years and the Sonny South
segments.title: Playing music for a living while still at school, until the day job in 1939
segments.summary: Turner explains he was still in school when he started playing professionally, then played music full time until 1939.

segments.chapter: Early years and the Sonny South
segments.title: Sonny South Syncopators personnel, 1928
segments.summary: He joined the ten- or eleven-piece reading band in 1928 and names its members: Leo Dejan, Gilly, Lee, Emile Fritz and others.

segments.chapter: Early years and the Sonny South
segments.title: How George Augustine hired him, rehearsals and WWL broadcasts
segments.summary: Augustine heard him at the Midway and hired him as a rhythm man. The band began broadcasting on WWL, though they made no records.

segments.chapter: Early years and the Sonny South
segments.title: Recordings with Celestin and with Peter Bocage
segments.summary: Turner recorded with Celestin's band, filling in for Jeanette Kimball, and made a record with Peter Bocage.

segments.chapter: Early years and the Sonny South
segments.title: Swapping with Jeanette Kimball for Celestin's tours; end of Prohibition; playing support
segments.summary: He swapped places with Jeanette Kimball so she toured with Celestin's band while he stayed in town with Sonny South. Prohibition's end hurt the big bands. He describes playing light, orchestrated rhythm piano.

segments.chapter: Early years and the Sonny South
segments.title: Ashton Murray, Sonny Johnson and Caesar as arrangers
segments.summary: Allen asks about Ashton Murray, who needed written music, and Turner names Sonny Johnson and Caesar as arrangers for the Sonny South band.

segments.chapter: Sonny South breakup and small bands
segments.title: Bocage brothers leave Sonny South, and the band reorganizes
segments.summary: Eddie Pearson and the Bocage brothers are discussed. A dispute led to firings and a rival band, and Turner kept the original Sonny South going with new players.

segments.chapter: Sonny South breakup and small bands
segments.title: George Augustine's role in the Sonny South band
segments.summary: Turner says Augustine was the original Sonny South man, possibly its manager, and that Richard McNeil came after him.

segments.chapter: Sonny South breakup and small bands
segments.title: Kid Rena's small band at the Gypsy Tea Room
segments.summary: After Sonny South he played piano in a four-piece band led by Kid Rena at the Gypsy Tea Room, nightly for two or three years, until large bands replaced them.

segments.chapter: Sonny South breakup and small bands
segments.title: Working with Paul Barnes, and the order of bands before Piron's
segments.summary: He worked with Paul Barnes after the Gypsy Tea Room, names the band and the Davis brothers, and sorts out when he played with Piron, Lavella and Willie O'Connor.

segments.chapter: Sonny South breakup and small bands
segments.title: Willie O'Connor's band at the Entertainers and Big Anderson
segments.summary: He describes Willie O'Connor's band (Cyril, Roy Evans, Big Anderson) and then Kid Kaifer's pickup groups.

segments.chapter: Sonny South breakup and small bands
segments.title: Playing with Kid Thomas; Elton Theodore ran the business and phone
segments.summary: He played early on with Kid Thomas's band, whose business Elton ran, and compares that to his own booking role for Sonny South.

segments.chapter: Sonny South breakup and small bands
segments.title: Kid Thomas's real name and musicians' nicknames
segments.summary: Talk about Joseph Butler as Kid Thomas and nicknames, including Whipple and Egg for Turner.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Three big New Orleans bands and playing with Sidney Desvigne and Nelson
segments.summary: He names the big bands (Celestin, Desvigne, Sonny South, Piron) and substitutes with Desvigne and Big Eye Nelson in the 1940s.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Creole Serenaders personnel and Peep Ducongé; Piron's band
segments.summary: After La Vida he played with the Creole Serenaders; its members are named. Talk then moves to the Ducongé family and Piron's band.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Tape pause and picking the story back up at La Vida
segments.summary: The speakers lose their thread and agree to return to La Vida.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: La Vida band lineup with Kid Howard and Jim Robinson
segments.summary: Turner names the musicians in the La Vida band, with its banjo and guitar players.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Working conditions and pay at La Vida taxi dance hall
segments.summary: The job ran nonstop; pay was low during the Depression with ten cents a dance. The hostesses worked on percentage.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: The Davis brothers who played at La Vida
segments.summary: Turner clarifies which Davis played drums at La Vida and how he relates to Jimmy Davis.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Back to Willie O'Connor's Entertainers band and Roy Evans
segments.summary: They return to the Entertainers band and its lineup, and talk about drummer Roy Evans, who played with Sam Morgan.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Handy's band and the Louisiana Shakers
segments.summary: They sort out the name Louisiana Shakers, and whether Turner played with Handy and Lewis Gibbon.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Kid Rena's Gypsy Tea Room band and its floor shows
segments.summary: Walter Delarue, George Augustine and Rena played there in the 1940s, and floor shows with a comedian and dancers were featured.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: No old photographs of himself; the comedian
segments.summary: Turner has no band pictures, only one individual photo, and recalls the comedian's jokes.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Going back to La Vida with Handy, about eight years
segments.summary: After the Entertainers he joined Handy at La Vida. Several band changes and a switch to a nightclub marked the roughly eight years there.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Day job with the light company from 1939
segments.summary: He began with the power company in 1939 and retired after 33 years.

segments.chapter: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
segments.title: Origin of the name La Vida, the owner, and substituting at the Budweiser
segments.summary: They discuss the name and owner of La Vida, how Handy hired him, and his Saturday work at the Budweiser.

segments.chapter: Day job, war and Bocage's band
segments.title: Joining Peter Bocage's band: personnel
segments.summary: Around the time of his day job he joined Bocage's six-piece band, whose members he lists and who later left or died.

segments.chapter: Day job, war and Bocage's band
segments.title: Short service in the army, 1943
segments.summary: Turner served only briefly in 1943, being over age.

segments.chapter: Day job, war and Bocage's band
segments.title: Bocage's demands on a piano player, his drummers and discipline
segments.summary: Bocage wanted a leading piano style and was strict about tempo, drinking and dress.

segments.chapter: Day job, war and Bocage's band
segments.title: What bands charged and uniforms
segments.summary: Turner talks about prices for band jobs and uniforms.

segments.chapter: Day job, war and Bocage's band
segments.title: Playing up and down for Bocage until the band ended
segments.summary: Bocage wanted a more active piano style. Turner stayed to the end of the band, his last.

segments.chapter: Big Eye Nelson, Lutton's and Adams
segments.title: Substituting with Big Eye Louis Nelson's four-piece band
segments.summary: He subbed for the band's pianist and then worked regularly with Nelson's four-piece, faking by ear. He left after a dispute over tips.

segments.chapter: Big Eye Nelson, Lutton's and Adams
segments.title: Working at Lutton's nightclub in the Depression
segments.summary: He describes the Lutton brothers, the beer-only crowd, strict order and the musicians who played there.

segments.chapter: Big Eye Nelson, Lutton's and Adams
segments.title: Jobs with the Adams brothers
segments.summary: After Lutton's he played piano for a group involving one of the Adams brothers near St. Charles.

segments.chapter: Big Eye Nelson, Lutton's and Adams
segments.title: The Bocage family band and Peter Bocage's manner
segments.summary: He discusses who played in the Bocage band, Eddie Pearson and Pete's harsh teaching, and prefers his own style.

segments.chapter: Celestin, arranging and learning music
segments.title: Celestin's band: arrangers and trumpet section, 1933-35
segments.summary: Turner names Celestin's arrangers and trumpets, and says he worked and traveled with the band between 1933 and 1935.

segments.chapter: Celestin, arranging and learning music
segments.title: Celestin band's saxes, bass, guitar and entertainer Joe Lawrence
segments.summary: He lists the rest of the Celestin lineup and the singer Joe Lawrence.

segments.chapter: Celestin, arranging and learning music
segments.title: Celestin's repertoire and the arranger Caesar
segments.summary: Celestin played mostly stock arrangements. Caesar arranged "Ring Them Bells".

segments.chapter: Celestin, arranging and learning music
segments.title: Turner's one arrangement and the Joe Robichaux recording
segments.summary: He arranged one number for Willie O'Connor, who recorded with Robichaux for Decca without release.

segments.chapter: Celestin, arranging and learning music
segments.title: Faking numbers and learning music from Manetta
segments.summary: He learned tunes quickly by ear. His teacher Manetta also set him on his first professional job.

segments.chapter: Celestin, arranging and learning music
segments.title: Wanting to play guitar
segments.summary: He tried guitar and would have liked the chord style of Charlie Christian.

segments.chapter: Celestin, arranging and learning music
segments.title: Regular bands and playing with Louis Dumaine
segments.summary: He lists his regular bands, mentions Sidney Desvigne, and says he worked with Louis Dumaine before Sonny South.
